definition: Aikuma is an Android app for collecting speech recordings with time-aligned translations.
details: The app includes a text-free interface for consecutive interpretation, designed for users who are not literate. The Aikuma won Grand Prize in the Open Source Software World Challenge (2013).

explainer.lead: Aikuma is an Android app for recording speech together with translations that stay aligned to the right moments in the audio. It helps fieldworkers gather larger collections of recordings from undocumented endangered languages, including in communities where participants may not read.

tiers.eli5: Aikuma is like a phone recorder that keeps a story and its translation matched up. Someone speaks, then another person explains what was said in another language, piece by piece. Because the app does not require reading, people who cannot read can still take part.
tiers.practitioner: Use Aikuma on Android phones to collect speech and human-produced, time-aligned translations through consecutive interpretation. Lig-Aikuma is the modified version for eliciting speech with text, images or videos. Plan for an interpreter and segmented recording rather than expecting automatic transcription or translation.
tiers.paperLevel: Aikuma is a mobile data-collection system whose core output can be represented as (speech audio, translation segments, alignment times), with translations produced through consecutive interpretation. Its text-free interface supports participants who are not literate. Lig-Aikuma separately extends the system with speech elicitation from text, images and videos.

explainer.example: In a remote village, a speaker records a story in an undocumented language. After each passage, an interpreter gives its translation, and Aikuma preserves the alignment so a researcher can later move between the original speech and the corresponding translated material.

usedIn.name: Usarufa language work
usedIn.detail: Aikuma was first used with this Papuan language in 2012; its name means "meeting place" in Usarufa.

usedIn.name: Endangered-language documentation
usedIn.detail: National Science Foundation-sponsored development aimed to collect more mobile-phone data than usual fieldwork allowed.

usedIn.name: Remote indigenous villages
usedIn.detail: Aikuma and Lig-Aikuma have collected substantial quantities of audio in these settings.

explainer.intuition: A recording is more useful for language documentation when a listener can find both what was said and its translation without losing their place in the audio. Aikuma combines recording and interpretation on a phone, without requiring participants to use text.
howItWorks: Record a speaker using an Android phone.
Have an interpreter provide a translation consecutively, after passages of speech.
Use the text-free interface so literacy is not required.
Keep the speech and translation time-aligned for later listening and language documentation.
explainer.whyItMatters: Mobile collection can gather more data on undocumented endangered languages than conventional fieldwork alone. The text-free design also makes participation possible for speakers and interpreters who are not literate.
misconceptions: Aikuma is not described as an automatic translator; its workflow uses consecutive human interpretation.
Its text-free interface does not mean it only records isolated words; it collects speech recordings with aligned translations.
Lig-Aikuma is a modified version with additional elicitation features, not the original app.
